A lazy dplyr table over an xarray variable or grid

Source: R/tbl.R
tbl_xarray.Rd

tbl(con, from) returns a lazy table over one variable, or over a grid of variables: dplyr verbs accumulate, and no data are read until dplyr::collect() (or a print, which shows a small preview). The verbs compile to a single Python statement, shown by dplyr::show_query() and run through DBI::dbGetQuery() like any other statement. Building it checks field names and probes coordinates, which needs Python, but reads no data.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'XarrayConnection'
tbl(src, from, ...)

Arguments

src

an XarrayConnection

from

a variable name (a data variable, or a coordinate); several data variables on one grid; or the name of a grid, as xr_grids() lists it (either view)

...

unused

Value

a lazy tbl_xarray; dplyr::collect() returns a tibble

Details

A grid is the set of variables on one set of dimensions (see xr_grids()), and a grid table has a column per member, as tidync's hyper_tibble() does: tbl(con, c("sst", "ice")) for some members, or tbl(con, "time,zlev,lat,lon") for a grid by its name. It compiles to a Dataset statement, ds[['sst', 'ice']], and the verbs apply as they do to one variable, with these differences:

  • select() decides which members are read: the statement names the selected members, plus any a filter needs (which are dropped after it). It must name at least one member.

  • the guard counts values, cells times members.

  • printing previews at most getOption("xrdbi.preview_members", 4) members, since each is at least a chunk read.

  • variables on different grids are refused, because a statement over both would repeat each value along the dimensions its variable lacks (a surface field across 37 pressure levels).

xr_chunks() takes a lazy table too, and maps what collecting it would read: for a grid table, a row per member read and chunk.

Supported verbs: filter(), select() (plain column names), head(), collect(), show_query(), and as.data.frame(). filter() takes ==, %in%, <, <=, >, >=, between() and & (or several arguments), each comparing a field with a value; there is no |, ! or !=. collect() is guarded like DBI::dbFetch(): above max_cells cells read (default getOption("xrdbi.max_cells", 1e7)) it errors unless collect(force = TRUE); as.data.frame() takes the same arguments and gives a plain data frame. Printing shows the first getOption("xrdbi.print_n", 6) rows, reading at most one chunk; options(xrdbi.print_preview = FALSE) turns the preview off.

Filters are pushed into xarray where they can be, and the rest applied after (the "residual"):

  • a filter on a dimension (==, %in%, or a range) compiles to an inclusive .sel(), so only the part of the array it selects (its "hull") is read; %in% is an exact .sel([...])

  • strict inequalities on a dimension use the inclusive hull, then a boolean .isel() on that dimension's index trims the boundary, so the result is still an xarray object

  • predicates on data variables, and mixed forms on one dimension, are kept as a pandas .query() applied Python-side, before conversion to R

  • predicates on non-dimension coordinates (2-D lat/lon of a curvilinear grid, a 1-D coordinate along time) stay in that query for exactness, but are checked against the coordinates at collect time and the read narrowed to the index block holding every passing cell (.isel() with literal slices, visible in show_query()). Dimensions without coordinates are pinned to their positions first (.assign_coords(y=range(n))), so they render as they would unfiltered

  • without such a query, head() and select() apply in R to the fetched rows, and head(n) first narrows the selection to the leading block that holds its n rows, so a peek at a huge variable reads one corner; dplyr::show_query() lists these R steps

  • at collect time each hull dimension is asked for its direction, and the slice is oriented to match: filter(latitude > 18, latitude < 19) works identically on ascending and DESCENDING coordinates

See also

XarrayResult for statements written in Python (and values passed with params); xr_query(); xr_grids() for the grids; the guard and preview options in xrdbi-package.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
## needs a Python environment with xarray (and here zarr, gcsfs)
library(dplyr)
con <- dbConnect(xarray(),
  "gs://gcp-public-data-arco-era5/ar/full_37-1h-0p25deg-chunk-1.zarr-v3",
  engine = "zarr", storage_options = reticulate::dict(token = "anon"))
u <- tbl(con, "100m_u_component_of_wind") |>
  filter(latitude > 18, latitude < 19, longitude >= 73, longitude <= 74,
         time >= as.POSIXct("1980-01-01", tz = "UTC"),
         time < as.POSIXct("1980-01-02", tz = "UTC"))
show_query(u)
collect(u)
## the store's time axis starts in 1900, its data in 1940
tbl(con, "2m_temperature") |>
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("1980-01-01", tz = "UTC")) |>
  head(3) |> collect()

## the surface grid: 262 members, of which select() reads three
xr_grids(con)
wind <- tbl(con, "time,latitude,longitude") |>
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2020-01-01 00:00", tz = "UTC"),
         time <= as.POSIXct("2020-01-01 05:00", tz = "UTC"),
         latitude >= -43, latitude <= -42,
         longitude >= 147, longitude <= 148) |>
  select(time, latitude, longitude, `2m_temperature`,
         `10m_u_component_of_wind`, `10m_v_component_of_wind`)
show_query(wind)
collect(wind)
xr_chunks(wind)   # 18 chunks: 6 hours, 3 members
} # }
